docs.title: 3C — security & code safety
docs.text: This is the page to forward to your security architect or platform-security lead. It deliberately under-claims — where 3C stops, it says so plainly, because that's the part that matters most to you.

docs.title: Where your code goes
docs.text: The developer workstation is the trust boundary. 3C ships Claude Code skills — everything it adds (the skills, rules, agents, the CLAUDE.md, and the records its workflow produces, such as handover and PR artefacts) is plain files in your own git repository. There is no backend and no telemetry at L1: nothing 3C adds leaves your repo or workstation, and 3C adds no new path off your machine for source code, prompt content, or credentials. It does not change how your AI assistant already talks to its model provider — that traffic is your existing behaviour, covered by your existing agreement with that vendor. (At L2+, the only thing 3C can optionally emit is anonymised metadata — counts, pass/fail, durations — to a self-hostable backend you run.)

docs.title: What defines the security posture
docs.text:
• OWASP-aligned generation. 3C ships security rule sets aligned to the OWASP Top 10 (VP-01-F04) — parameterised queries, input validation, output encoding, secure credential handling — applied at the point of generation, before code reaches review.
  • Secret-scanning at write boundaries. Every skill that writes files scans for secrets before the write lands; credentials never get committed by an AI session that 3C governs.
  • Security review skill. /review (VP-02-F03) applies a team security checklist (injection, authn/z, crypto, dependency risk) with severity ratings, so AI-assisted changes get a consistent security pass.
  • Local-first by construction. Config and event state live on the workstation (SQLite + JSONL). No code or prompt content is persisted off-box; the developer workflow never blocks on a backend, and L2+ telemetry queues locally with no always-on egress dependency.

docs.title: What L2 adds for security — shipped May 2026 (v1.5.0)
docs.text:
L2 extends the security posture along four axes — every one of them still local-first, every one of them additive to (not replacing) your existing security tooling:

  • CWE Top 25 alongside OWASP Top 10. The L1 OWASP pack stays. L2 adds a CWE-mapped security rule set so AI-assisted code generation sees both lenses at once — the OWASP "what an attacker exploits" framing and the CWE "what weakness was introduced" framing. Reviewers get the explicit OWASP↔CWE mapping in the rule rationale.
  • Security Scan Gate as a pre-commit hook. SAST + dependency-vulnerability scan runs per commit, with team-configurable severity thresholds. Refuses the commit on critical findings; warns and proceeds on lower severities. Writes a JSONL event regardless of outcome — so bypass patterns are visible in the audit log without relying on developers to self-report.
  • security-reviewer subagent shipped at L2. A dedicated Claude Code subagent your team's AI can dispatch when touching auth, crypto, or input-handling code paths. Tool allowlist declared in the agent's frontmatter; sandboxed by Claude Code's platform layer; cannot read .env*, ~/.ssh/, or ~/.aws/ per the path-guard hook (verifiable in src/agents/path-guard.ts).
  • PM-tool token handling keeps the credential out of the skill. L2's /3c-create-issue reaches Jira / Linear / GitLab through an in-process adapter registry; GitHub stays on the gh CLI path. The token is resolved per call, handed straight to the adapter, and never written to disk by the framework, cached in process, or returned in tool output. A bundled MCP server was the original design for this boundary (AD-11); it was retired in the 2026-08 consolidation without changing where the credential lives, because it never held it.

What L2 still does NOT do — and the same honesty discipline applies:

  • L2 is not a SAST replacement. The Security Scan Gate shifts severity-thresholded SAST left into the commit lifecycle, but it does not absolve you of your existing SAST programme.
  • No telemetry egress at L2. Every hook telemetry event is local JSONL on the developer workstation. The L3 team backend is self-hostable when it lands; at L2 your event log does not leave the workstation. If your security architecture requires "no data leaves the device" — L2 satisfies it by construction, not by configuration.
  • No new credential paths. L2 adds no places your team's credentials are written, persisted, or transmitted. Keychain is the only credential boundary; if your OS keychain is compromised, every credential on the workstation is compromised — 3C does not introduce a new exposure.

What 3C does NOT do

3C is a developer-productivity and standards-alignment framework, not a compliance product. It does not certify any standard, issue a conformity statement, or produce a regulatory evidence pack — that is a separate, future business case, not part of L1–L4. 3C is not a SAST replacement: it shifts secure-coding defaults left, it does not absolve you of your existing security review and scanning.

docs.title: Evaluate it as OSS, not as a vendor
docs.text:
3C is MIT-licensed. There is no vendor to assess, no data-processing agreement to negotiate, and no telemetry you did not opt into. Evaluate it as OSS, not as a vendor — the way you evaluate any open-source dependency:

  • Licence: MIT — read it in the repo LICENSE.
  • SBOM: 3C ships as the npm package @kgn-git/3c. Generate a software bill of materials with standard tooling — npm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx (npm's built-in SBOM) or cyclonedx-npm — run in your project after install, so it captures 3C plus its transitive dependencies in context. Because 3C is git-installed (tag-pinned), the SBOM records it with a git+https provenance reference rather than a registry version — that is the accurate supply-chain provenance, not an anomaly. There is no bespoke 3C command to trust; it is the standard ecosystem path.
  • Source of truth: every claim on this site is grounded in the public distribution repo kgn-git/3C; evaluators can start a discussion to walk the requirements baseline with the maintainers.

docs.title: 3C — for developers
docs.text:
This page is for the IC sitting in front of Claude Code today. Not your manager, not your CISO — you, the person who will actually use this thing every commit.

We'll be honest about what changes for you and what doesn't. 3C is built on the principle that the worst thing a governance framework can do is slow you down. So everything below is designed around two questions: what new thing do I have to think about? and what gets faster?

docs.title: What changes on day one
docs.text:
After npx 3c init, npx 3c skills install, and npx 3c hook install (run npx 3c doctor to confirm they landed), three things are different in your daily flow:

  1. Your AI assistant has read the team's conventions. npx 3c init writes a CLAUDE.md into the repo root with your team's standards distilled into a single file under 150 instructions. The AI will spontaneously follow them. You will stop reviewing PRs where the AI used a pattern your team retired six months ago.
  2. A pre-commit hook runs before every commit. npx 3c hook install registers it: lint, types, unit tests, secret scan — under a 10-second budget on a typical repo. Catches the obvious before your reviewer has to.
  3. Four slash commands appear in Claude Code. npx 3c skills install copies them in: /3c-create-issue, /3c-implement, /3c-review, /3c-test. Each runs the standardised version of those workflows for your team. You can ignore them — the L1 standards still apply through CLAUDE.md — but they're the fastest path through the same lifecycle that everyone on your team is now running.

That's L1. It's enough for a long time.

docs.title: What L2 adds for you specifically
docs.text: L2 — v1.5, shipped May 2026 — is where 3C starts paying you back for the conventions L1 captured. Here's what starts mattering for you:

docs.title: Pre-commit gates that catch the obvious before review
docs.text:
Beyond L1's lint / types / unit-tests / secret-scan baseline, L2 adds three more gates that fire automatically before code review:

  • Post-Edit Validation runs the moment Claude Code finishes an edit — checks the change against the layer-boundary rules your team declared. Catches "the AI imported from internal/" in ~300ms, before you've even staged the file.
  • Security Scan Gate runs SAST + dependency-vulnerability scan per commit. Refuses on critical findings; warns on lower severities. You get the warning in the same buffer as the test failures — no separate dashboard to check.

All gates write a JSONL event regardless of pass / fail / bypass, so the picture stays complete even when you 3c bypass --reason="hotfix" to ship a critical change.

docs.title: The boundary gate — and the command that drafts its config
docs.text:
The boundary gate is the one check in 3C that enforces your architecture rather than ours: .3c/architecture.yaml declares your layers and, under deny, the import directions you forbid. Run npx 3c arch-check check at your commit gate or in CI and it exits non-zero when a change crosses one, naming the file, the line, and the direction — "domain" layer must not import from "infra" layer. (With nothing staged — the usual CI checkout — it checks the whole tracked tree, so adopt it on a baseline you have cleaned.) These rules live in that YAML file, not under .claude/rules/; the rule id in the output is layer-boundary — and it is the same rule set the post-edit validator applies live: one file, two moments, the assistant's edit and your commit. npx 3c setup scaffolds the file inert — all comments, checking nothing — because nobody but your team knows your layers.

You don't have to write it by hand. npx 3c arch-check discover reads your repo's tracked import graph (it walks git ls-files, so stage or commit your JS/TS source first) and drafts the config from how your code actually depends on itself: directory clusters are grouped into dependency tiers, which become your layers, and each upward direction — a lower tier importing a higher one — becomes a deny pair, so the draft never flags the code you have right now. The layer names it emits are deliberately generic (tier-0, tier-1, …): rename them to what your team calls those layers — in both layers and the deny pairs — prune what you don't want, and once the draft has at least two layers the gate is live. If nothing in your tree imports across a directory boundary — everything under one directory, or several that never reference each other — you get a single layer and no deny pairs; the command says so, and the gate stays quiet until your imports span more directories. On a repo with no tracked multi-directory JS/TS source there is nothing to cluster yet: the draft says so and, when it is your active config, keeps the worked example for hand-editing, and the gate stays inert until source lands. When your architecture.yaml parses to real layers, the same command writes .3c/architecture.proposed.yaml beside it and leaves your rules untouched.

docs.title: The why behind every rule — it lives in the rule file
docs.text:
The annoying part of inheriting someone else's standard is a rule with no reasoning attached. L2 keeps the reasoning where the rule is.

Every rule is a plain markdown file under .claude/rules/, versioned with the repo, so the standard and its reasoning travel together: the bundled OWASP pack cites its source on the rule itself, and your team's own rules accumulate their "why" through the PRs that change them — the review thread is the provenance. Open any rule file and you're reading the standard itself, not a summary of it.

docs.title: Your AI assistant gets two more agents
docs.text:
L1 shipped code-reviewer and test-author as subagents your AI can dispatch. L2 adds two more:

  • architect — for "I'm about to make a design decision and want a second opinion that knows our ADRs and patterns."
  • security-reviewer — for "I'm touching auth / crypto / input-handling and want the OWASP + CWE lens applied before I PR this."

Both are plain Markdown files under .claude/agents/ with declared tool allowlists — you can read them, fork them, change them. No black box.

docs.title: The crew — multi-lens review and orchestrated delivery, on demand
docs.text:
Those agents started as something your AI dispatches one at a time. The L2 surface then grew the roster to eight (adding product-owner, ux-expert, qa-reviewer, journey-architect) and wired them into a crew you drive with three explicit commands — they only run when you type them:

  • /3c-review-board — run the whole panel over your branch before you open the PR. The eight specialists each report findings; the board reconciles them into one verdict — blocking, advisory, or clean — de-duplicating what they agree on and flagging where two disagree on severity for you to settle. The reconciliation is tested code (3c reconcile), so the same diff gives the same verdict every time — not a model mood.
  • /3c-project-manager — hand it an issue and it drives the whole pipeline: enrich → plan → test-first → review board → PR. It checkpoints before it branches or opens a PR, and it never merges, force-pushes, or bypasses a hook on your behalf. You stay in control of anything irreversible.
  • /3c-programme-manager — when your work spans several projects in one workspace (a monorepo, or sibling folders), it sequences them in dependency order with a checkpoint between each, reading the ledger at .3c/dependencies.yaml.

The verdict is always advisory — you decide. Run npx 3c doctor if you ever wonder whether the crew installed cleanly; it checks all eight agents and three orchestrators are wired.

docs.title: Cross-platform workflow skills
docs.text:
If your team uses Jira Cloud, Linear, or GitLab Issues instead of GitHub: /3c-create-issue now routes to all four. Token via OS keychain (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows, Secret Service on Linux). Nothing cached, nothing returned in tool output, nothing committable as a secret.

If your test runner is Mocha, Playwright, or JUnit (not just Jest / Vitest / Pytest): /3c-test recognises those too, and writes in that runner's idiom. It does not generate test bodies from your source — it requires a test that fails on its assertion before the implementation exists, and the review board rejects an assertion that cannot fail.

docs.title: Narrowed test runs that never fake a green
docs.text:
Inner TDD iterations don't need the whole suite. /3c-implement's inner loop asks npx 3c test select which tests the current changeset needs — and you can run it yourself when you're driving the loop by hand. It prints the command(s) worth running and the reason it chose them, because a narrowed run must never be silent about being narrowed. The reason to care is the failure behaviour, not the speed-up:

  • Git unreadable? Full suite. If it cannot read the changeset from git, it escalates to running everything instead of presenting "nothing changed".
  • Typo in a flag? An error. A flag it doesn't recognise is rejected, not silently ignored.
  • Unmapped input? Wider, not narrower. Anything the test map doesn't cover widens the run, and /3c-implement, which drives it, treats "no test files found" as a failure, never a pass.

The pre-PR gate still runs everything, by rule.

docs.title: Your own local insights dashboard
docs.text:
L2 captures hook telemetry to .3c/events/*.jsonl — local-only, gitignored, never egressed at L2. The Personal Local Insights Dashboard renders it as a static HTML file: run npx 3c dashboard in your terminal, then open .3c/dashboard.html in your browser:

  • Which rules fire most for you (so you know what to internalise).
  • How often your commits pass the gate on first try (so you know whether the team's standards are sinking in).
  • The post-edit validation deltas trend (so you can see your own AI-assisted-quality curve).
  • What shipped, read from your repository's handover issues through gh and cached locally (so you can see delivery, not just gate runs).

It's the developer's mirror of what the L3 team-backend dashboard will roll up across the team — but at L2, your telemetry does not leave your machine, and nobody else sees it. The delivery view only reads your repository's handover issues from GitHub, which anyone with access to the repository can read anyway.

docs.title: What L2 does NOT change for you
docs.text:
The framework is designed to disappear when it's not needed. So:

  • You can still bypass. npx 3c bypass --reason="hotfix for prod" — run in your terminal, not as a slash command — skips the hook chain for the next commit. Logged in the JSONL events; never silently suppressed.
  • You can still edit by hand. The post-edit validator only fires when Claude Code is the editor. Editing a file directly in your IDE bypasses it — same as if the file didn't have rules. (This is intentional; 3C governs AI-assisted change, not human IDE work.)
  • Your model interactions don't change. Whether Claude Code is talking to Sonnet, Opus, or a local model — 3C sits between you and the editor, not between Claude Code and its provider. Your existing model-traffic agreement is undisturbed.
  • You don't have to learn a new tool. The four L1 slash commands plus /3c-onboard, /3c-retrospective and the crew orchestrators (/3c-review-board, /3c-project-manager, /3c-programme-manager) all live where every other Claude Code skill does. A few things are terminal commands rather than slash commands — npx 3c dashboard, npx 3c bug and npx 3c bypass --reason="…" among them — run them in your shell, not in Claude Code.

docs.title: How to adopt L2 if you're already at L1
docs.text:
Realistically, half a day of focused work for the IC who's championing it:

  1. npm install --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha> — pin the release by its commit sha (listed at github.com/kgn-git/3C/releases); a tag can be moved, a sha cannot.
  2. npx 3c setup --replace — one command provisions everything (CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks, the L2 skills, the crew agents product-owner/ux-expert/qa-reviewer, an inert arch-check), then runs 3c doctor to verify. Use --replace when upgrading an existing tree: without it, every file you already have is skipped, so a skill that changed upstream stays stale. It overwrites local edits — commit .claude/ first and read git diff after. The individual init / skills install / agents install / hook install commands still run on their own if you prefer to step through.
  3. npx 3c doctor — re-check anytime. It flags both directions of skew: a stale 3c CLI that's behind your installed skills (upgrade the CLI), and installed skills that still invoke a retired command because your CLI moved ahead of them (re-install with --replace). It also names orphaned skills and agents that no longer ship at all, which only a manual delete can clear.
  4. Enable one gate at a time and watch the JSONL events accumulate for a few days before turning on the next. Recommended sequence: Post-Edit Validation → Security Scan Gate.
  5. After a week, run npx 3c dashboard and open .3c/dashboard.html to see your own data.
  6. After shipping a piece of work, optionally capture a retrospective with /3c-retrospective <scope> — a single-project, evidence-based retro that is a suggestion, never a gate.

docs.title: 3C — for engineering leaders
docs.text:
3C — Claude Code Coach — is built by one architect with a public steward. That's not a confession; it's how we keep retros tight and decisions auditable.

This is the page to forward when you're making the case for a rollout to a CTO or a board. It answers the four questions that usually come up: what it costs, what it buys, what happens if the architect steps away, and how you reverse it.

docs.title: What L1 costs you
docs.text:
• Adoption time: one week — a focused adoption sprint — from npx 3c init to the whole team's assistants sharing a spine. The standards / workflow / quality baseline is captured on day 1 and the delta measured by end of week, so the rollout proves itself inside the sprint rather than on faith.
  • Infrastructure: none — L1 runs on developer workstations. No backend, no service to operate, no data-processing agreement.
  • Vendor lock-in: none. The workflow skills conform to the Agent Skills open standard and the licence is MIT — fork it, keep it, replace it.
  • Ongoing maintenance: a steward role of ~2 hr/week per active 6–15-developer team — curating rules from retrospectives, not babysitting infrastructure.

docs.title: What L1 buys you
docs.text:
Anchored to the three pillars — and these are the measured end-of-adoption-week deltas the sprint captures (convention-consistency on AI-authored diffs; the share of changes moving through the /3c-* skills; the pre-commit gate pass-rate and what it caught pre-review), not promises that mature on faith. They are visible by the end of the adoption week and compound from there:

  • Standards layer → by the end of the adoption week, two engineers on the same repo produce structurally consistent code without a reviewer forcing it. Architectural drift stops compounding.
  • Workflow layer → by the end of the adoption week, issue-creation, implementation, review, and test authoring run the same way on every laptop — onboarding a new hire is reading one CLAUDE.md, not shadowing for a month.
  • Quality layer → by the end of the adoption week, lint/types/tests/secret-scan run before code review, every commit — the review queue stops absorbing what a gate should have caught.

docs.title: What L2 adds — shipped May 2026 (v1.5.0)
docs.text:
L2 is the Automate level. Same install, same .claude/ footprint, same reversal posture — but the standards your team agreed to at L1 now enforce themselves before code review.

For the eng-leader audience, the things to forward up:

  • The gate chain becomes automatic. Post-Edit Validation runs at the point of AI generation (~300ms); the Security Scan Gate runs pre-PR; the Architecture Boundary Enforcer blocks dependency-direction violations at the commit gate. Every gate is independently disable-able and writes a JSONL event regardless of pass / fail / bypass. The review queue stops absorbing what a gate should have caught — and you can prove it from the events log without asking developers.
  • Every rule stays traceable to its origin. A rule is a plain markdown file under .claude/rules/ that travels with the repo: the bundled OWASP pack cites its source on the rule itself, and your team's own rules carry their reasoning through the PRs that change them — provenance you audit from git history, not from a database beside it. When a junior asks why one of the team's own standards exists, the answer is in the repo — the rule file and the PR thread that shaped it — instead of an interruption to a senior.
  • The PM-tool integration is not GitHub-only. /3c-create-issue routes to Jira Cloud, Linear and GitLab Issues through an in-process adapter registry, and to GitHub through the gh CLI. The bundled MCP server that once wrapped the registry was retired in the 2026-08 consolidation. The token is resolved per call, never cached and never returned in tool output. Same skill UX across all four.
  • Your team owns the copy, not a fork. npx 3c skills install copies the skills and agents into your repo under git as /3c-*, against the upstream kgn-git/3C source. Your team evolves them in pull requests like any other code, without forking a maintained dependency.
  • Your senior-review process, made consistent. The L2 surface grew a multi-agent crew that runs the review-and-delivery process your best engineers run by hand — the same way on every change, regardless of who is at the keyboard or what hour it is. /3c-review-board convenes eight specialist reviewers (architecture, code, security, tests, product, UX, QA, customer-journey) and reconciles their findings into one deterministic verdict — blocking, advisory, or clean — with genuine disagreements surfaced for a human rather than averaged away. /3c-project-manager carries an issue through that review on the way to a PR; /3c-programme-manager does it for a dependency-ordered chain of projects across one workspace. Every verdict is advisory and every git action is checkpointed — the crew accelerates the process, it does not take the decision. It is also the bridge to L3: these per-change verdicts are exactly what the L3 dashboards roll up.

What L2 does NOT change:

  • No backend, no telemetry egress. L2 events are local JSONL on the developer workstation. There is still no 3C-hosted service, no opt-in tier, no telemetry pipe to a vendor. L3 introduces a self-hostable backend; L2 does not.
  • No new vendor lock-in. Still MIT, still Agent Skills standard, still git-installable, still git revert-removable.
  • No compliance or regulatory framing. That business case is parked. L2 is a developer-productivity and team-quality layer, full stop.

The L2 adoption sprint is the same shape as L1: one focused week from npm install ...#v1.5.0 to measurable deltas. The three metrics it captures: pre-PR gate pass-rate, post-edit validation findings per AI-authored diff, and the boundary findings arch-check records at the commit gate. If you're at L1 and your team is ready for the next level, the L2 today page is the technical brief; this page is the business one.

docs.title: Bus-factor and succession
docs.text: Here's how succession works in this project — the steward role is documented and transferable; fork rights are explicit (MIT); contributor pathway is open via GitHub Discussions; any structural change to project governance will be announced in an ADR before code lands. We do not yet have a named succession plan; we have a succession process.

docs.title: The architect
docs.text: 3C is maintained by one architect with a public steward, working in the open at github.com/kgn-git — public role, public commit history, public contributor pathway via GitHub Discussions. The full public bio (name, role, contact) is steward-reviewed and confirmed by the architect before public launch, per this page's non-negotiable verification gate — it is not auto-generated. What is verifiable today is the work itself: every decision is an ADR, every sprint a handover, every change a reviewed PR.

docs.title: L3 backend commercial intent
docs.text: L3 introduces a self-hostable backend dependency. No commercial entity, hosted offering, or paid tier is planned at this time. If that changes, it will be announced in an ADR before any code lands.

docs.title: Reversal in one PR
docs.text: L1 is reversible. To remove 3C entirely: git revert the PR that added .claude/ (or git rm -r .claude/ && git commit). What remains afterward: nothing of 3C's — the .claude/ tree is the entire footprint. No daemon to uninstall, no global package, no workstation state, no backend to decommission. The codebase is exactly what it was, minus the conventions you chose to keep.

docs.title: 3C — get started
docs.text:
Two routes, depending on where you are. Fresh install for a project adopting 3C for the first time; update to latest for an existing deployment moving to the current release. Both sit at the current release — there is nothing older to pin.

Current release: v2.1.1. 3C ships as a private, git-installed package from kgn-git/3C — there is no public npm package to install.

docs.title: Fresh install
docs.text:
A new project, adopting 3C for the first time. From the project root:

npm install --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha>
# <release-sha>: the commit sha listed for that version at github.com/kgn-git/3C/releases
npx 3c setup            # one shot: CLAUDE.md + rules + hooks + skills + agents + arch-check, then doctor

If npm stops with EALLOWGIT. npm 12 refuses to fetch a git dependency unless you allow it, which is why the command above passes --allow-git=root. root allows every git dependency your own package.json names, and none further down the tree. npm 10 and 11 accept the flag without a warning.

Every later npm ci or npm install in this project needs the same permission. To stop passing the flag, add this line to the project's .npmrc and commit it:

allow-git=root

The line covers every git dependency your package.json names, now and later. If you would rather not grant that standing permission, pass the flag on each command instead.

3c setup is a thin sequencer over the individual commands (init, rules install, hook install, skills install, agents install, arch-check init, doctor) — each still runs on its own if you would rather step through it. Everything lands in your repo under git; nothing is installed globally and nothing phones home.

Running in CI, a container or a script, with no terminal to answer prompts? Plain npx 3c setup detects that and takes the wizard's defaults, printing which ones it used. --yes asks for the same thing explicitly and stays quiet about it:

npx 3c setup --yes      # accepts defaults; no prompts

Neither form overwrites a CLAUDE.md, skill or agent you already have. Overwriting is always a flag you pass: npx 3c setup --replace refreshes skills, agents and rules (setup never touches CLAUDE.md), and npx 3c init --merge rewrites CLAUDE.md with your new answers, keeping a backup of the old one — run it in a terminal to choose different answers. On Windows Git Bash, use PowerShell, cmd or winpty.

Verify at any time:

3c --version            # should report 2.1.1
3c doctor               # confirms the install and flags anything missing

docs.title: Update to latest
docs.text:
An existing L1/L2 deployment moving to the current release. Two steps: refresh the CLI, then refresh the project.

1. Upgrade the CLI. The 3c command and the skills it installs evolve together, so a stale CLI is the most common cause of "command not found" or a crew skill silently degrading. Reinstall the global CLI at the current release:

npm uninstall -g @kgn-git/3c
npm install -g --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha>
3c --version            # should report the release you pinned

2. Refresh the project. Upgrading the CLI does not rewrite the skills, agents, and rules already copied into a project. Plain 3c setup only adds what is new — it skips every file that already exists, so a skill whose contents changed upstream stays exactly as it was. To pick up changed skills and agents you need --replace. Commit .claude/ first: --replace overwrites every skill and agent that still ships upstream, so any local edits are lost.

git add -A .claude && git commit -m "checkpoint before 3c setup --replace"
3c setup --replace      # refreshes changed skills/agents, not just missing ones
git diff HEAD -- .claude   # review what changed; re-apply any local edits
3c doctor               # confirms the installed artefacts match the upgraded CLI

3c doctor closes the loop in both directions, which matters because they need opposite repairs:

  • CLI older than your skills — a skill invokes a command your 3c binary lacks. Upgrade the CLI (step 1 above).
  • CLI newer than your skills — a skill still invokes a command that has been retired. The binary moved on; your copy-installed markdown did not. Repair with 3c skills install --replace / 3c agents install --replace (which is what 3c setup --replace runs for you).

Doctor also reports orphaned artefacts — a skill or agent under your 3c- prefix that no longer ships at all. No install command can clear those, because the installer only ever copies files that still exist upstream; delete them by hand once you have checked nothing local depends on them.

docs.title: Install traps to avoid
docs.text:
• npm i -g 3c installs an unrelated public package, not this one — never use it.
  • npm i -g @kgn-git/3c fails with E404: the package is private and git-only. Install from the git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha> URL above — by commit sha, because a tag can be moved and a sha cannot.
  • If a command still resolves to an old build, a project-local copy is shadowing the global — run Get-Command 3c (PowerShell) or which 3c. A node_modules/.bin/3c inside a project takes precedence over the global binary; upgrade or remove that local install too.

Removing 3C instead? It is a git revert plus a couple of local deletions — see uninstall. Choosing which maturity level to adopt? Start with the maturity model.

docs.title: 3C — what L1 ships today
docs.text: L1 is the Standardise level: every team member's AI assistant follows the same conventions, the same workflow skills, and the same pre-commit gates. This is the honest scope page — what you get in week one, and what you deliberately do not.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
npm install --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha>
# <release-sha>: the commit sha listed for that version at github.com/kgn-git/3C/releases
npx 3c init

npx 3c init writes .claude/CLAUDE.md. Then npx 3c rules install, npx 3c hook install, npx 3c skills install, and npx 3c agents install layer in the standards substrate, the pre-commit gate, the workflow skills, and the starter subagents — each copied into your repo under git. Finish with npx 3c doctor to confirm the install is coherent. The one-shot npx 3c setup runs all of it in a single command — full routes (fresh install and update to latest) are on Get started.

Rollback

git revert of one PR removes 3C from your project. The .claude/ tree is plain version-controlled files — no daemon, no global install, no workstation state to unwind.

docs.title: The 9 L1 features
docs.text:
L1 brings nine features across the three layers — each one chosen because it makes a daily difference, not to fill a matrix.

Everything L1 scaffolds into .claude/ — real files, not a roadmap. One git revert removes all of it.

Standards layer

  • CLAUDE.md Generator — a CLI wizard that produces an optimised CLAUDE.md inside the 150-instruction cognitive budget.
  • Rules Distribution Engine — git-based .claude/rules/ with glob matching and version-controlled sync.
  • Architecture Pattern Library — pre-built rule sets for Clean Architecture, Hexagonal, and Layered MVC.
  • Security Policy Templates — OWASP Top 10 aligned rules for secure code generation.

Workflow layer

  • Issue Creation Skill — /3c-create-issue, structured issue creation.
  • Feature Implementation Skill — /3c-implement, the standardised TDD development workflow.
  • Code Review Skill — /3c-review, the team review checklist with severities.
  • Test Authoring Skill — /3c-test, tests written test-first, following team conventions.

Quality layer

  • Pre-Commit Hook Engine — PreToolUse hooks running lint, typecheck, unit tests, and secret scan under a 10-second budget.

docs.title: The L1 gate chain — what runs before a code review
docs.text:
L1 ships with one PreToolUse hook registered in .claude/settings.json by 3c hook install that runs four checks in sequence before every AI-assisted commit. The whole chain completes in <10s for repos under 500 files (NFR-PERF-01).

L1 runs four checks in one hook. The chain blocks the commit on failure — there is no override flag at L1; the bypass path is 3c bypass --reason="…", run in your terminal, with the reason logged.

The four checks, in order:

  1. Lint — your project's configured linter (ESLint, Pylint, etc.) runs on the touched files. Style and basic static analysis catch the "locally optimal, globally incoherent" patterns that AI assistants produce when six engineers each chase their own taste.
  2. Types — your project's type-checker (TypeScript tsc --noEmit, mypy, etc.) runs on the touched files. A passing unit suite over code that does not compile is a lie the test runner tells you.
  3. Unit tests — your project's unit suite runs against the touched modules. The narrowest fast signal — if these fail, nothing downstream runs.
  4. Secret scan — every file written or edited by an AI session that 3C governs is scanned for credentials before the write lands. Catches accidental commits of AWS access keys, GitHub tokens, database URLs, etc.

L1's hook is blocking. If any of the four checks fails, the commit is refused. This is the conscious L1 trade-off: simple, predictable, no telemetry-driven advisory layer. The escape hatch is npx 3c bypass --reason="<one-line>" — a terminal command, not a slash command — which logs the bypass and proceeds — but the bypass is recorded, not silent.

docs.title: What L1 does NOT have
docs.text:
The honesty discipline carries over from the rest of this page. L1 is not L2. The following gates ship at L2 and are not part of the L1 hook chain:

  • Post-Edit Validation — runs the moment Claude Code finishes an edit (~300ms), checking the dependency direction you declared in .3c/architecture.yaml before the file is even staged.
  • Security Scan Gate — SAST plus dependency-vulnerability scan with severity-thresholded refusal.
  • Architecture Boundary Enforcer — static analysis of dependency direction per .3c/architecture.yaml.

If you need any of those, upgrade the pin and then refresh the copied artefacts — npx 3c init alone rewrites CLAUDE.md and leaves your skills and agents untouched, so anything that changed upstream stays stale. The full route (including what --replace overwrites) is on get-started → update to latest. See also what L2 ships today.

docs.title: The 4 workflow skills
docs.text:
Each ships as an Agent Skill at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Previews:

# /3c-create-issue
name: create-issue
description: Create structured GitHub issues with team-template
  population. User-only skill; not auto-invoked by the model.
Guides you through a well-structured GitHub issue. Does not auto-attach code, environment, or system state — the issue content is exactly what you provide.

# /3c-implement
name: implement
description: Standardised feature-implementation workflow — fetch
  issue, plan, branch, TDD-loop, review, PR. Asks for confirmation
  before each external-state-changing step. Never auto-merges,
  never force-pushes, never bypasses hooks.
Explicit-invocation only. Walks an issue from fetch → plan → branch → TDD loop → review → PR with a destructive-operation interlock.

# /3c-review
name: review
description: Apply a team-specific static review checklist to the
  current branch's diff against main. Read-only, local-only —
  structured findings with file/line, severity, suggested fix.
Read-only: never modifies files, never calls the network, never echoes credentials. Produces a pre-PR findings report.

# /3c-test
name: test
description: Write unit or integration tests test-first, following
  team conventions, for whatever framework the project uses. Detects
  the framework from package configuration, reads conventions from
  .claude/rules/, and writes a test that FAILS before the
  implementation exists.
Never overwrites existing tests; the first write per session asks for confirmation.

docs.title: The pre-commit hook engine
docs.text:
One synchronous orchestrator runs every configured gate before a commit lands — lint, typecheck, unit tests, secret scan — inside a 10-second budget on a 500-file repo. A failed gate blocks the commit with a remediation message; an emergency bypass is available and audited. The full delegation chain and gate sequence:

What L1 feels like in a normal working day.

docs.title: What L1 deliberately does NOT include
docs.text:
L1 is intentionally small and reversible. Here's what it deliberately leaves for later — each paired with the level that owns it, so nothing is a surprise:

  • No telemetry — that is L2.
  • No dashboards — that is L3.
  • No audit evidence packs — that is L3.
  • No policy-as-code — that is L4.
  • No cross-platform adapters — that is L3.

Each capability is paired with the maturity level that owns it. See the maturity model for the portfolio framing and the commitment each level carries.

docs.title: 3C — what L2 ships today
docs.text:
L2 is the Automate level: every L1 standard your team agreed to is now enforced by a hook before code review, every time. L1 made conventions explicit. L2 makes them stop being aspirational.

This is the honest scope page for L2 — what you get when you upgrade from L1, and what L2 still deliberately does not do.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
npm install --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha>
# <release-sha>: the commit sha listed for that version at github.com/kgn-git/3C/releases
npx 3c setup            # one shot: CLAUDE.md + rules + hooks + skills + agents + arch-check, then doctor

3c setup is a thin sequencer over the individual commands (init, rules install, hook install, skills install, agents install, arch-check init, doctor) — each still runs on its own if you'd rather step through it. Everything lands in your repo under git. The current release is v2.1.1 on the same kgn-git/3C repo as L1; existing L1/L2 deployments upgrade in place — re-run 3c setup --replace. Plain 3c setup adds only what is missing and skips every file that already exists, so a skill whose contents changed upstream would stay stale; --replace overwrites them, so commit .claude/ first and review the diff afterwards:

npm install --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha>
npx 3c setup --replace  # refreshes CHANGED skills/agents; without --replace they are skipped

Installing for the first time, or moving an existing project to the current release? Both routes — with the traps to avoid — are on Get started.

Reversal posture is unchanged from L1

git revert of one PR still removes 3C from your project. L2 adds local JSONL telemetry events to .3c/events/ and a SQLite config file — both gitignored, both reversible by removing the directory. No daemon, no global install, no workstation state to unwind.

docs.title: What's new in L2 — the 14 features
docs.text:
L2 brings 14 features layered on top of L1's 9. Grouped by the layer they extend:

Everything L2 adds is layered on the L1 substrate — same .claude/ tree, same git revert reversal, more capability per commit.

Standards layer — three additions

  • Dynamic Context Loader — loads only the rules relevant to the file types and directories under work, so the 150-instruction budget holds even as your rule library grows past it.
  • Architecture pattern library extension — microservices and modular-monolith packs alongside L1's clean-architecture / hexagonal / layered-mvc.
  • Security pack extension — cwe-top-25 alongside L1's OWASP Top 10, with mappings between the two so reviewers see both lenses at once.

Quality layer — four new gates

  • Post-Edit Validation — PostToolUse hook firing the moment Claude Code finishes an edit, validating the layer-boundary rules your team declared before the change is even staged.
  • Security Scan Gate — SAST + dependency-vulnerability scan per commit, with severity thresholds. Refuses the commit on critical findings; warns and proceeds on lower severities.
  • Architecture Boundary Enforcer — static analysis of dependency direction per .3c/architecture.yaml. Catches the "module A reaching into module B's internals" pattern at commit time.
  • Hook Telemetry — every hook run writes a .3c/events/*.jsonl event with pass/fail, timing, and rule attribution. The L2 substrate for everything observability-related downstream — local-only, no egress at L2.

Workflow layer — four additions

  • Bug Report command (npx 3c bug, run in your terminal — not a slash command) — captures the environment (OS, runtime, project state, recent commits, scrubbed env vars) into a structured report — no more "works on my machine" reproduction archaeology.
  • Onboarding Skill (/3c-onboard) — guided codebase orientation with per-developer progress tracking. Pause/resume across sessions; local state, no cloud account needed.
  • Multi-PM Adapter — /3c-create-issue now routes to Jira Cloud / Linear / GitLab Issues alongside the L1 GitHub path. Token via OS keychain only, never cached, never returned in tool output.
  • Test framework extension — Mocha / Playwright / JUnit recognised alongside L1's Jest / Vitest / Pytest, so /3c-test writes in the runner your project already uses.

DX & observability layer — three additions

  • Role-tailored onboarding (/3c-onboard --role <frontend|backend|devops>) — role modules are appended to the project-derived roadmap, so a role gets the team's own CLAUDE.md and scripts as well as its own sequence. Same pause/resume. This shipped as a separate onboard-guide skill and was folded into the onboarding skill, which is why the count above is unchanged.
  • Extended starter subagents — architect and security-reviewer subagents alongside L1's code-reviewer and test-author. All four still under the 150-instruction CS-02 budget (npm run cs02 audits it).
  • Personal Local Insights Dashboard — run npx 3c dashboard to write the local-only .3c/dashboard.html, showing your own hook telemetry: which rules fire most for you, how often your changes pass review on first try, and the boundary findings arch-check has recorded. Its delivery view reads your repository's handover issues through an installed, signed-in gh, cached locally; offline, it shows the last rows it fetched and says so. Telemetry never leaves the workstation. The local mirror of what the L3 team backend will roll up across the team.

docs.title: The L2 gate chain — what runs before a code review
docs.text:
Solid arrows are what a hook or gate runs at L2 — none is aspirational. Dashed arrows are the developer's own steps: staging the change, opening a rule file, returning to the edit.

In a typical L2-adopting team's commit lifecycle, 3C runs three gate types automatically:

  1. PostToolUse — Post-Edit Validation (~300ms) — the moment Claude Code finishes an edit, validates the layer-boundary rules your team declared against the relevant file.
  2. PreToolUse — Pre-Commit Hook (<10s) — lint, types, unit tests, secret scan.
  3. Pre-PR — Security Scan Gate (<60s typical) — SAST + dependency vulnerabilities.

Each gate is independently disable-able. Each writes a JSONL event regardless of pass / fail / skip — so the picture is complete even when a gate is bypassed under npx 3c bypass --reason="..." (a terminal command, not a slash command).

docs.title: The multi-agent crew — your team's development process, automated
docs.text:
The gate chain enforces standards on every commit. The multi-agent crew, added to the L2 surface after v1.5, goes one layer up: it automates the process your team runs around the code — issue enrichment, planning, test-first implementation, multi-lens review, and delivery — as a panel of specialist agents coordinated by explicit orchestrator skills. It is the part of senior-engineer judgement that usually lives in people's heads, written down and made repeatable.

One change in; eight lenses; one deterministic verdict out. The reconciliation is tested code, not a model summary — and the verdict is advisory: a human still decides.

Eight specialist agents. Each is a focused, read-only reviewer that Claude Code auto-selects by description and runs in its own context:

  • architect — boundary direction, coupling, ADR adherence.
  • code-reviewer — correctness, readability, team conventions.
  • security-reviewer — the OWASP / CWE lenses, secret and trust-boundary checks.
  • test-author — test coverage and convention adherence (the one writer on the panel).
  • product-owner — scope, priority, and maturity-level fit.
  • ux-expert — screen-level usability, accessibility, and UI copy.
  • qa-reviewer — acceptance-criteria traceability and edge cases.
  • journey-architect — customer-journey reachability: can a user still reach every capability and recover from every state.

The first four shipped with L1/L2; product-owner, ux-expert, qa-reviewer, and journey-architect complete the eight-agent crew. All install as 3c-* (3c-architect, …) and stay within the 150-instruction CS-02 budget (npm run cs02 audits it).

Three orchestrator skills drive them. These are explicit-invocation only — you type them; Claude never auto-runs them:

  • /3c-review-board — convenes the panel on a change, then reconciles their findings deterministically into one verdict: blocking, advisory, or clean. It de-duplicates the findings agents agree on, surfaces where two agents disagree on severity for a human to settle, and ranks the rest. The reconciliation is tested code (3c reconcile), not a model's free-text summary — identical inputs always produce the same verdict.
  • /3c-project-manager — drives one issue through the whole pipeline: enrich → plan → test-first implementation → review board → ship. It is checkpointed — it confirms before creating a branch or a PR, and it never auto-merges, force-pushes, or bypasses a hook.
  • /3c-programme-manager — coordinates delivery across the projects in one workspace (a monorepo's packages, or several folders in one checkout). It sequences work in dependency order, runs the project-manager pipeline per project with a checkpoint between projects, and maintains a provenance-bearing dependency ledger at .3c/dependencies.yaml.

An optional /3c-retrospective skill captures what worked and what didn't after you ship — a suggestion, never a gate. npx 3c doctor verifies the crew is installed coherently — all eight agents present, all three orchestrators wired, no stale references — so a half-installed crew shows up before you lean on it.

This is the L1→L2→L3 arc made concrete: L1 wrote the standards down, L2 enforced them at the gate, and the crew runs the review and delivery process a senior engineer would run by hand. It stays honest about its limits. Every verdict is advisory — a human still decides. The orchestrators never touch git without confirmation. And it is fully local: no backend, and no nested agents — the platform runs each specialist one level deep from a main-thread skill. Rolling these per-change verdicts up across the team is the L3 observability story — see maturity model.

docs.title: What L2 still does NOT do
docs.text:
L2 keeps the L1 honesty discipline: it under-claims, and it names limits.

  • No backend, no telemetry egress. Every L2 event is local JSONL on the developer workstation. There is no 3C-hosted service, no opt-in tier, no telemetry-to-vendor pipe. The L3 team-backend story is mapped — see maturity model — but at L2 your data does not leave the workstation.
  • No cross-team observability yet. The personal local insights dashboard shows your hook telemetry. Roll-up to team / repo / programme level is L3 work.
  • No policy-as-code or governance-as-code. Standards are still defined as rules + skills + agents, edited by humans, reviewed via PR. The L4 "governance that adapts to complexity" story is horizon — not L2.
  • No compliance / regulatory framing. The compliance business case is parked — see strategy/parked/compliance-business-case.md upstream. L2 is a developer-productivity and team-quality layer, not a regulatory evidence pack.
  • No vendor lock-in added at L2. Still MIT, still Agent Skills standard, still git-installable, still removable with one git revert.

docs.title: How to adopt L2
docs.text:
If you're already at L1, the upgrade is a focused half-day:

  1. npm install --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha> — pin the new release by its commit sha (listed at github.com/kgn-git/3C/releases).
  2. npx 3c init — idempotent; re-runs against your existing .claude/ tree, refreshing CLAUDE.md.
  3. npx 3c skills install --replace && npx 3c agents install --replace — re-copy the workflow skills and the crew agents under your slug (picks up the new crew orchestrators and the product-owner / ux-expert / qa-reviewer agents). --replace is what refreshes a skill that changed; without it both commands skip every file you already have. Commit .claude/ first — it overwrites your local edits.
  4. npx 3c hook install — re-registers the PreToolUse + PostToolUse hooks (you may need to confirm the diff once).
  5. npx 3c doctor — confirm the result is coherent: every skill and agent prefixed, every hook registered (PreToolUse and PostToolUse), no stale references. A fail on hooks means step 4 has not been run against this workspace.
  6. Give the boundary gate something to check: npx 3c arch-check discover drafts your layers and deny pairs from the repo's own import graph. Until layers exist, neither the commit gate nor the post-edit hook has anything to check. Post-Edit Validation is registered by step 4 and runs from then on — advisory only, it never blocks an edit. To waive a layer pair, the advisory prints the exact arch-check except command, and that waiver is honoured by both the hook and the commit gate. A suppress: list in .3c/validation.yaml silences paths for the post-edit advisory only — the commit gate does not read it, so a path silenced there will still block at commit time.
  7. Run an L2 adoption sprint — same one-week shape as L1, just measuring different deltas. The three metrics that prove L2 is working: pre-PR gate pass-rate, post-edit validation findings per AI-authored diff, and the boundary findings arch-check records at the commit gate.

If you're new to 3C, start at what L1 ships — L1 is a fine place to stay for a long time, and L2 layers on it cleanly when you're ready.

docs.title: See it from your seat
docs.text:
• A developer's view of L2 → for developers
  • An engineering leader's view → for engineering leaders
  • A security architect's view → security & code safety

What we're learning

The L2 sprint shipped 21 features across 6 sprints with 1256/1256 tests green at merge; seven have since been retired, leaving the 14 listed above. The full per-feature handover record is maintained upstream — every decision is traceable. If you're evaluating, the rationale is there: start a discussion.

docs.title: 3C — the maturity model as a portfolio plan
docs.text: L1 → L4 isn't a checklist to complete. It's a set of places a team can choose to be, each answering a real question and each carrying its own, clearly-stated level of commitment. Adopt only the level whose risk you actually need to retire — and stay there as long as it serves you. Most teams find L1 is plenty for a long time.

docs.title: Locate your team
docs.text:
Three yes/no questions. No JavaScript — expand the answer that matches.

1. Do two engineers using AI on the same repo produce structurally consistent code without a reviewer forcing it?

No → you are at L0. What you need next: L1 (Standardise) — shared conventions in every AI's context. Start at what L1 ships today.

Yes → you are at least L1. Continue to question 2.

2. Are your quality gates (lint, types, tests, secrets) run automatically before code review, every time?

No → you are at L1. What you need next: L2 (Automate) — the gates stop being aspirational.

Yes → you are at least L2. Continue to question 3.

3. Can you show, with data, how AI is affecting your team's quality and velocity — and where the ROI is?

No → you are at L2. What you need next: L3 (Observe) — telemetry becomes dashboards: quality trends, velocity, process adherence, ROI.

Yes → you are at L3+. L3 (Observe) and L4 (Optimise) are on the roadmap — under active study, not yet available. What they aim at: dashboards and ROI attribution (L3), then governance that adapts to change complexity (L4).

docs.title: The four levels
docs.text: You can stop at any level. Stopping is not "incomplete adoption" — it's a decision.

docs.title: L1 — Standardise
docs.text:
Shipped — May 2026

  • The question it answers: Is our team's AI converging or diverging?
  • Business risk addressed: architectural drift — every AI session locally optimal, globally incoherent.
  • Commitment level: Reversible — one PR to remove.
  • Calendar anchor: internal — adopt in one week (a focused adoption sprint), on your team's own calendar.

docs.title: L2 — Automate
docs.text:
Shipped

  • The question it answers: Is our quality bar automatic or aspirational?
  • Business risk addressed: review-burden inflation — humans hand-checking what a gate should catch.
  • Commitment level: Rebuildable — telemetry can be disabled.
  • Calendar anchor: internal — paced to your team's quality-debt curve. A focused half-week adoption sprint from install to measurable deltas.

L2 adds 14 features layered on top of L1's 9: extended rule families (CWE Top 25, microservices, modular-monolith), automated quality gates (Post-Edit Validation, Security Scan Gate, Architecture Boundary Enforcer, Hook Telemetry), workflow expansions (Bug Report, Onboarding, Multi-PM adapters, extended test frameworks), and DX additions (the role-tailored onboarding roadmap, since folded into the onboarding skill as --role, extended starter subagents architect + security-reviewer, Personal Local Insights Dashboard). The L2 surface then grew a multi-agent crew — eight specialist review agents (architect, code-reviewer, security-reviewer, test-author, product-owner, ux-expert, qa-reviewer, journey-architect) coordinated by three orchestrator skills (/3c-review-board for a reconciled multi-lens verdict, /3c-project-manager for the per-issue delivery pipeline, /3c-programme-manager for dependency-ordered delivery across a workspace's projects). It automates the review-and-delivery process a senior engineer runs by hand, and its per-change verdicts are the raw material the L3 layer rolls up. The full inventory and adoption path: what L2 ships today.

docs.title: L3 — Observe
docs.text:
Roadmap — not yet available. Under active study; the specification is being refined from adopter feedback. No release date.

  • The question it aims to answer: Can we see, with data, how AI is affecting our quality, velocity, and ROI?
  • Business risk it targets: decision-blindness — scaling AI-assisted change with no measured view of its quality and velocity impact.
  • Direction: telemetry captured at L2 becomes team-observability dashboards — quality trends, velocity/DORA, ROI, process adherence, a cross-project view.
  • Want to shape it? L3 is where adopter input matters most — tell us what you'd need to see.

docs.title: L4 — Optimise
docs.text:
Roadmap — not yet available. The furthest-out level; under study, its shape will be refined from adopter feedback as L3 lands. No release date.

  • The question it aims to answer: Is our governance adapting to our complexity?
  • Business risk it targets: governance ossification — one-size rules taxing simple changes, under-guarding complex ones.
  • Direction: a closed loop where telemetry feeds retrospectives that evolve standards, with complexity-adapted governance and policy-as-code.
  • Want to shape it? Start a discussion — the earlier the input, the more it counts.

What we're learning

Teams tell us the hardest part is deciding not to climb a level they don't need yet. If you're weighing that, we're happy to think it through with you: start a discussion.

docs.title: Skills vs Agents
docs.text: 3C ships two kinds of extension that are easy to confuse. They are invoked in completely different ways.

docs.title: The one-line model
docs.text:
• Skills are user-invoked slash commands — you type them (/3c-review).
  • Agents (subagents) are dispatched workers — a skill, or Claude itself, hands a bounded task to one via the Task tool. You never type an agent as a slash command.
Skill Agent Lives in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md .claude/agents/<name>.md Invoked by you, as /3c-<name> a skill / Claude, via the Task tool Selected how you choose it (or, if model-invocable, Claude may auto-run it) by matching the agent's description, or named by a skill Runs in the main conversation a fresh, isolated context window List them 3c skills list 3c agents list

docs.title: Why agents aren't slash commands
docs.text: An agent is a specialist persona (e.g. a read-only reviewer) that runs in its own context so it can do focused, bounded work — a long diff scan, a security pass — without crowding the main thread. Because they're a delegation mechanism, not a command mechanism, they have no slash form. To use one explicitly, ask in plain language ("use the code-reviewer subagent on this diff"), or run the skill it's paired with.

docs.title: Worked example: /3c-review → 3c-code-reviewer
docs.text:
1. You run the skill: /3c-review.
  2. The skill dispatches the 3c-code-reviewer subagent (read-only: Read, Grep, Glob) for the long-context diff scan, in a fresh context.
  3. The subagent returns structured findings; the skill formats and prints them.

You typed one thing (/3c-review); the agent ran underneath it. The shipped agents — 3c-architect, 3c-code-reviewer, 3c-security-reviewer, 3c-test-author — are each paired to a skill this way.

docs.title: Namespace
docs.text: Commands install under the hyphen prefix /3c-<skill>. Run 3c skills list to see exactly what's installed and how each is invoked.

docs.title: Orchestration convention (composing the crew)
docs.text:
Some skills are orchestrators: they convene several specialist agents and combine their output. Because a subagent can never spawn another subagent, the orchestration always lives in a skill (the main thread), not in agent-to-agent calls. The convention any orchestrator follows:

  1. Dispatch one level deep, in parallel. The skill issues one Task call per specialist agent in a single turn, each in a fresh context. No agent dispatches another agent.
  2. Collect findings in the shared schema. Each agent returns a fenced json array of { severity, category, message, file?, line?, suggestion? }.
  3. Reconcile deterministically. The skill assembles { "<agent>": [findings] } and pipes it to 3c reconcile, which de-dupes, merges cross-agent agreement, ranks, flags conflicts, and returns one verdict. Reconciliation is tested code, not prose, so the verdict is reproducible.
  4. Stay read-only / local unless the skill explicitly owns a checkpointed write step.

/3c-review-board is the worked example: it dispatches 3c-code-reviewer, 3c-architect, 3c-security-reviewer, 3c-qa-reviewer (and 3c-ux-expert for UI changes) in parallel, then reconciles. Teams can compose their own boards or pipelines from the installed agent roster by following these four steps.

docs.title: 3C — uninstall
docs.text:
3C installs by copying into your repo and a small global CLI. That makes removal honest: it is a git revert plus a couple of local deletions. Nothing phones home, so there is no account to close and no remote state to purge.

Installing or upgrading? Both routes — fresh install and update to latest, with the traps to avoid — are on Get started.

docs.title: Moving to a later release
docs.text:
There is no separate upgrade command. The dedicated verb that used to do this is retired (#396): it ran git verify-tag against the package directory npm installs without a .git, so for a project-local install git walked up and verified the adopter's own repository rather than the framework's. It refused for every adopter it was meant to serve.

Re-install the release, then refresh the copied artefacts:

npm install --allow-git=root git+https://github.com/kgn-git/3C.git#<release-sha>
# <release-sha>: the commit sha listed for that version at github.com/kgn-git/3C/releases
npx 3c setup --replace   # backs up every file it overwrites to .3c/backups/
npx 3c doctor            # reports any skill still invoking a retired command

npm 12 refuses the install without --allow-git=root. Pass the flag as above, or add allow-git=root to the project's .npmrc; Get started says why.

The second step is not optional. Installing the package moves the CLI; it rewrites nothing under .claude/. On its own it moves you to a release where a command may have been retired while your installed skills still instruct it — which is precisely what doctor reports on. Your BRAND_* config is preserved across the refresh.

--replace overwrites every skill and agent that still ships upstream. Before it overwrites a file whose content differs, it copies it into .3c/backups/<timestamp>/ (git-ignored) and prints where — an edit is one copy away from recovery. Commit .claude/ first anyway, and review git diff .claude/ afterwards.

What is and is not verified. The integrity of what you install rests on the commit sha you pin: a tag can be moved to a different commit, a sha cannot, and npm records the resolved sha in your package-lock.json, so npm ci reinstalls exactly that commit. 3C does not verify a signature on the package — nothing checks that the commit you pinned is a genuine release other than where you copied the sha from (the release notes on github.com/kgn-git/3C). Signed releases are planned for when 3C is productised.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Because 3C is copied into your repo under git, the cleanest removal is to revert the install:

git revert <install-commit-or-PR-merge>

That takes the standards, skills, agents, and hooks back out in one reversible step — the reversal posture the rest of the site promises. If you would rather remove the artifacts directly, delete what the installers wrote:

  • .claude/skills/, .claude/agents/, .claude/rules/ — the copied workflow skills, crew agents, and rule packs.
  • the PreToolUse hook entries in .claude/settings.json — the orchestrator + path-guard (git revert removes them if they were committed; otherwise edit the file).
  • CLAUDE.md (and the companion CLAUDE.local.md.example + the .gitignore lines init added).
  • the .3c/ directory — architecture and hook config plus all local state: events/*.jsonl telemetry, the local SQLite config, onboarding data, and dashboard.html.

Then remove the global CLI:

npm uninstall -g @kgn-git/3c

There is nothing else to unwind. No daemon, no global workstation state, no remote account. The L2+ telemetry is gitignored local JSONL and SQLite under .3c/ — it never left your machine, so removing the directory removes the data. git revert of one PR restores the project exactly as it was.

docs.title: Why teams are reaching for this now
docs.text:
A lot of engineering teams are having the same conversation right now. One instinct is to pause AI assistants until there's a policy; another is to keep shipping with them and hope review catches what matters. Both are understandable, and both tend to get uncomfortable over time.

There's a calmer third path, and it's the one that also happens to hold up when the codebase gets big and the team gets busy: keep your team's AI work aligned, deliberately and lightly.

docs.title: The quadrant nobody tooled
docs.text:
Think about code quality as a 2×2. One axis: individual versus team. The other: pre-AI versus AI-assisted.

Pre-AI AI-assisted Individual Linters, IDE hints, code review — mature, twenty years of tooling Copilot-class autocomplete, per-developer prompts — maturing fast Team Style guides, architecture review boards, shared conventions — mature — empty —

Three of the four quadrants have decades of tooling. The fourth — keeping a team's AI-assisted work coherent — has almost none. That empty quadrant is where the cost is accumulating, and it stays invisible until a refactor, an incident, or a new hire walks into it and asks why six files solve the same problem six different ways.

docs.title: AI engineering alignment
docs.text:
The discipline that fills that quadrant needs a name, because you cannot budget for a problem you cannot say out loud. Call it AI engineering alignment: the practice of keeping every team member's AI assistant working from the same conventions, the same workflow, and the same quality bar — so that the team's output is coherent even though no two prompts are ever identical.

It is not prompt engineering; that is an individual craft. It is not an MLOps concern; no models are being trained here. It is a software-process discipline, and it lives in the gap between "we adopted AI" and "we can defend how we adopted AI." Naming it matters because the unnamed version gets filed under "developers will sort it out" — and they will, badly, one inconsistent merge at a time.

docs.title: Locally optimal, globally incoherent
docs.text:
Here is the failure mode without the discipline. Each developer's AI assistant is, in isolation, doing a good job — passing the local tests, matching the file it can see, shipping the feature on time. Every session is locally optimal. But no single session can see the team's conventions, the architecture decisions made in last quarter's review, or the security baseline that currently lives in one senior engineer's head. So the aggregate is locally optimal, globally incoherent: six valid-looking implementations of one pattern, three subtly different error-handling styles, an architecture that drifts a degree with every sprint until the map no longer matches the territory.

This is not a model-capability problem — it is a context-distribution problem. Frontier models degrade past roughly 150 distinct instructions, so you cannot fix incoherence by pasting the entire standards document into every prompt; the context has to be earned per phase, not dumped in wholesale. (Claude Code Coach treats that 150-instruction wall as a hard budget; the full explainer is a follow-on.) The teams that win the next two years are not the ones with the best prompts. They are the ones whose assistants share a spine.

This is a multi-step journey — L1 is a complete, useful place to be on its own.

docs.title: The forcing function is AI velocity itself
docs.text:
If the engineering argument feels deferrable, the adoption curve will close the window for you. AI assistants are being rolled out across teams now, not in some future quarter — and every unaligned session compounds the empty-quadrant cost faster than a human-paced team ever accrued it. Drift that used to take a year of hand-written code now lands in a single sprint of AI-accelerated merges. The teams that align early pay a one-week adoption cost while the divergence is still small; the teams that wait pay it back as a refactor whose size grows with every AI-assisted commit.

That is the real "why now": AI makes the empty quadrant expensive on the timetable of your own adoption — the faster you ship with AI, the faster unaligned drift accrues, and the more a late correction costs.

docs.title: What this looks like in practice
docs.text:
Keeping AI coding aligned is not a committee and not a moratorium. It is conventions distilled into the assistant's context within a hard budget, a workflow every developer's assistant follows the same way, and quality gates that run before code review rather than after it. It is reversible — one revert removes it — and it is local-first, so no source code leaves the workstation to make it work. The maturity model lays out how far an organisation can take that and exactly what each step commits to. The full thesis, in engineering register rather than this leader-register summary, lives in the project's internal Vision document.

The argument is not "AI coding is dangerous, slow down." It is the opposite: AI coding is fast, and unaligned speed at team scale is how you arrive at the wrong place sooner. Alignment is what turns individual velocity into team progress.

docs.title: What we are NOT
docs.text:
Naming a category invites overclaiming, so the boundaries are explicit:

  • We are NOT an AI model or a coding assistant. 3C governs the assistants you already use; it does not replace Claude Code, Copilot, or Cursor.
  • We are NOT a compliance product. 3C is a developer-productivity and standards-alignment framework; regulatory/compliance positioning is a separate, future business case (parked — see strategy/parked/compliance-business-case.md), not part of L1–L4.
  • We are NOT a cloud service that ingests your code. 3C — Claude Code Coach — is local-first; source code never leaves the developer workstation to make it work.
  • We are NOT a productivity tracker. What 3C measures at L2+ is process adherence and quality, anonymisable and opt-in; it is not individual-developer surveillance.
  • We are NOT a one-time setup. 3C is a maturity model — the value compounds because each retrospective writes the next rule; a frozen install is an abandoned one.

What we're learning

This "why now" framing comes from real adoption conversations — yours may land differently. If the velocity pressure isn't what you're feeling, tell us what is: start a discussion.

docs.title: Prompt: "A day in the life of a developer using 3C" — infographic
docs.text: Source material on disk: site/index.html, site/why-now.html, site/maturity-model.html, site/l1-today.html, site/l2-today.html, site/for-developers.html, site/branding.html, docs/infographic/sdlc-infographic.html (the visual template — in-repo only; it is unpublished as of #354 and is being re-authored under #365), site/infographic/diagrams/*.mmd (existing mermaid sources), site/diagrams/{day-with-3c,journey,pillars}.svg.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Produce a multi-page, print-ready HTML infographic titled "A day in the life of a developer using 3C." It tells the working day of one engineer (call her Maya) who is shipping inside a team that has adopted 3C — Claude Code Coach at L2, and it makes the workflow legible at a glance: one phase per page, one diagram per phase, one key message per phase.

The deliverable is a standalone .html file that mirrors the structure, design system, and print posture of docs/infographic/sdlc-infographic.html (in-repo; unpublished per #354) — same A4 portrait pages, same typography, same colour tokens, same badge / title / diagram / key- message / footer rhythm — so the new infographic sits next to the existing one as a sibling deliverable, not a one-off.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: A new engineer joining a team that already runs 3C at L2. Assumes general familiarity with Git, sprint-based agile workflows, TDD, and PR review, plus everyday use of Claude Code as her AI assistant — but zero prior knowledge of 3C itself, its slash commands, its rule files, its subagents, or its gate chain.

docs.title: Hard constraints — Maya never edits code or tests by hand
docs.text:
This is non-negotiable, and the writer must read this section before starting the diagrams.

Maya is an instructor, not a typist. Every code change, every test change, every fix, every refactor in this infographic happens through Claude Code (her AI assistant) or through one of the /3c-* slash commands — never by Maya opening a file in her IDE and editing it manually. This is true even for:

  • writing the assertions in a TDD test (she prompts /3c-test or Claude Code with the assertions she wants in natural language; the skill or the assistant types them)
  • fixing a failing test (she re-prompts Claude Code with the diagnosis, or dispatches the architect / code-reviewer subagent for a second opinion, and lets the assistant apply the fix)
  • tightening an issue body that came back too vague (she iterates with /3c-create-issue until it is right)
  • correcting a boundary violation flagged at post-edit (she re-prompts Claude Code with the finding the validator reported)

Maya does type freely in three places, and only these three:

  1. Prompts — to Claude Code, to the slash commands, to subagents.
  2. Issue / PR comments in GitHub.
  3. Config-style decisions — picking the next issue, choosing a branch name, approving a destructive-operation prompt with y, running 3c bypass --reason="..." for a real hot-fix.

If a phase seems to demand hand-editing, that is a signal the phase is under-specified — re-prompt or re-dispatch instead. The infographic should reinforce this discipline visibly: in every diagram, the arrow that changes code is labelled with the slash command or the assistant that did the typing.

docs.title: What to establish on the cover page
docs.text:
Before the six phase pages, a cover page establishes:

  • The premise. 3C is AI engineering alignment: keeping every team member's AI assistant working from the same conventions, the same workflow, and the same quality bar. Without it, every session is locally optimal but the aggregate is locally optimal, globally incoherent (site/why-now.html).
  • The three pillars — Standards (CLAUDE.md under a hard 150-instruction cognitive budget, .claude/rules/, the architecture pattern library, the security policy templates), Workflow (the slash commands), Quality (the gate chain). site/diagrams/pillars.svg may be inlined or recreated as a small inset.
  • The L2 surface area Maya uses today — slash commands /3c-create-issue, /3c-implement, /3c-review, /3c-test, 3c bug, /3c-onboard (with --role), 3c bypass; the crew orchestrators /3c-review-board, /3c-project-manager, /3c-programme-manager; the eight review agents architect, code-reviewer, security-reviewer, test-author, product-owner, ux-expert, qa-reviewer, journey-architect; gate chain Post-Edit Validation (< 300 ms) → Pre-Commit (< 10 s) → Security Scan Gate (< 60 s).
  • Boundary enforcement — the post-edit hook checks every file the assistant writes for dependency-direction violations against the team's declared .3c/architecture.yaml and advises at write time; the arch-check gate records the same findings, and they surface in the dashboard's Boundary findings panel.
  • The honesty discipline — 3C deliberately under-claims; reversal is git revert of one PR; no source code leaves the workstation.

docs.text:
The infographic is 9 A4 portrait pages, in this order. (#516 dropped the batch phase — /3c-create-issue has no batch mode — and re-pointed sprint assembly to /3c-project-manager; the phases after it moved up one.)

docs.text:
The visual brief is exactly the existing infographic's stylesheet — do not invent a new design language. The writer should re-use:

  • A4 portrait pages, 210 × 297 mm, with padding: 14mm 14mm, page-break-after: always; cover and closing get padding: 18mm 16mm.
  • Fonts: Inter (300/400/500/600/700/800/900) for everything, JetBrains Mono for tags, badges, page numbers, and prompt/event snippets. Both from fonts.googleapis.com.

Indigo for orchestration and skills; amber for shared-context / rationales / advisories; emerald for quality gates passing; red (#FEE2E2 / #DC2626 / #7F1D1D) for failure / refusal states.
  • Per-page chrome: a .page-header with a left-side .badge (mono-font, 01 · INTAKE style) and a right-side .page-num (1 / 7); an H2 .diagram-title (~26pt, weight 800, letter-spacing -0.02em); a .diagram-subtitle (~12pt); the .diagram-wrap (use .tall for sequence diagrams, .xl for the Phase 4 state machine); a .key-message indigo-tinted box at the bottom (.key-label mono uppercase + .key-text 13.5pt weight 500); a .page-footer with the phase name on the left and a rule / artefact reference on the right.
