The writer should literally open docs/infographic/sdlc-infographic.html, copy its <style> block wholesale, and adapt only what the new content requires (e.g. adding a small "post-edit advisory" callout style and a prompt/snippet style).

docs.title: Diagram requirements — one per phase
docs.text:
All diagrams are mermaid sources. The writer should commit a .mmd file per diagram into site/infographic/diagrams/ following the existing naming pattern (f-intake.mmd, g-enrichment.mmd, i-sprint-assembly.mmd, j-implement.mmd, k-sprint-throughput.mmd, l-uat.mmd, m-dashboard.mmd), pre-render each to SVG with the same toolchain (puppeteer.config.json is already in the folder), and inline the SVGs into the HTML at the <!--SVG_F--> style placeholders.

Every mermaid source must begin with the same %%{init: ...}%% theme block the existing five diagrams use, so the typography and palette match. Pick the right diagram type per phase:

docs.title: Diagram F — Phase 1 — Intake → issue creation (flowchart TD)
docs.text: Nodes: PM Brief, Slack Thread, CSV (customer feedback) → /3c-create-issue prompt → iteration loop → GitHub Issue (structured: title, user-story, scope, out-of-scope, ACs, deps, source- link). Label the iteration arrow Maya re-prompts /3c-create-issue explicitly. Annotate the GitHub Issue node with the 6 required fields as a sub-list. Footer reference: L2 Multi-PM adapter · GitHub default at L1.

docs.title: Diagram G — Phase 2 — Technical enrichment (sequenceDiagram)
docs.text: Actors: Maya, architect (subagent), the rule file (.claude/rules/), GitHub Issue. Steps: Maya dispatches architect with the issue context; architect returns affected components / approach / risks / open questions / complexity / testing strategy; Maya reads, identifies one proposed pattern that doesn't fit the codebase, opens the rule file for the standard she's not sure about, pushes back to architect with the rule's own reasoning, gets a revised analysis, appends it to the GitHub Issue. Critical: no node labelled "Maya edits the analysis" — every change to the analysis is made by architect after Maya's prompt or by /3c-implement later.

docs.title: Diagram I — Phase 3 — Sprint assembly (flowchart TB)
docs.text: /3c-project-manager plan "<milestone>" above five coherence checks, named as the shipped skill's sprint-readiness gate names them: Contradictions, Shared surfaces, Dependency order, Duplicate or overlapping scope, Load-bearing assumptions. Four feed a coherent sprint (merged, sequenced, rewritten); one finding is held for a human to resolve or defer — the gate stops rather than guessing. (Until #516 this diagram showed /3c-review "adapted for sprint scope" — a flag that skill never had; it reviews a branch diff.)

docs.title: Diagram J — Phase 4 — One issue, end-to-end (stateDiagram-v2)
docs.text: The most detailed diagram — give it the .xl diagram-wrap class. States, in order: Issue selected → /3c-implement plan → branch created → /3c-test writes a failing test → Claude Code implements → Post-Edit Validator (~300ms) → loop back to Claude Code on failure, with the layer-boundary advisory naming the two layers → git stage + commit → Pre-Commit Hook (<10s) (lint / types / unit / secret) → loop back on failure with the failing check named → Security Scan Gate (<60s) → /3c-implement PR description → /3c-review-board → eight-agent panel (architect, code-reviewer, security-reviewer, test-author, product-owner, ux-expert, qa-reviewer, journey-architect) → reconciled verdict (blocking / advisory / clean) → Maya prompts Claude Code to apply the applicable findings → merge to main. Show the verdict as advisory — Maya still decides. Every edge that changes code is labelled with who typed it (Claude Code applies, /3c-implement applies, /3c-test writes) — never Maya.

docs.title: Diagram K — Phase 5 — Working the rest of the sprint (flowchart TD)
docs.text:
A compounding loop: Issue 2 → Issue 3 → Issue 4, each running through a compact box labelled /3c-implement (full loop, see Diagram J). Off to the side, three loops that get tighter each iteration: - Boundary loop: a layer-boundary advisory on issue 2 (an app → infra import the assistant wrote) → a clean run on issue 4 once the declared direction is second nature. - Pattern-reuse loop: prompt to /3c-implement references the merged PR ("follow the shape of #1284") — no re-pasting of standards into context (annotate 150-instruction budget held). - Subagent loop: architect dispatched once for a hard design call; security-reviewer dispatched before PR for an auth-touching change.

A side-branch shows the hot-fix path: prod incident → 3c bypass --reason="prod hotfix #INC-417" → JSONL event recorded → ship → follow-up issue auto-created.

A second side-branch shows the tricky-failure path (this is the one to design carefully so it stays consistent with the hard constraint above): Pre-Commit fails on tricky test → Maya reads the failing assertion → Maya prompts Claude Code: "the rule is right, the test asserts the wrong contract, regenerate it" → Claude Code revises the test → gate passes. No node labelled "Maya edits the test in IDE" — instead, the diagram makes visible that the rule's authority routes the fix through the assistant, not around it.

docs.title: Diagram L — Phase 6 — Manual end-user testing (sequenceDiagram)
docs.text: Actors: Maya, /3c-test, the team's deploy script, Staging environment, 3c bug, GitHub Issue. Sequence: Maya invokes /3c-test for the UI change → the skill writes the integration test test-first (test-author subagent assists) → Maya runs the team's own deploy script against staging → its pre-flight checks run → health check passes → Maya walks the acceptance criteria manually in staging → finds a regression → Maya runs 3c bug in her terminal → it captures OS, runtime, project state, recent commits, scrubbed env vars → files a structured bug issue → Maya links it from the original issue. Annotate the production-deploy arrow with the team's own approval.

docs.title: Diagram M — End-of-day reflection (pie or flowchart)
docs.text:
A small mock-up of the Personal Local Insights Dashboard at .3c/dashboard.html, written by npx 3c dashboard (a terminal command). Three panels: - Gates that fired most for me today (top 5 list) - First-try gate pass-rate (one big number, e.g. "78%") - Post-edit validation deltas trend (sparkline placeholder)

Annotate plainly: local-only · gitignored · never egressed at L2 · your manager cannot see this.

docs.title: Phase narratives — body copy under each diagram
docs.text:
The diagram carries the structure; the body copy (placed inside the .diagram-subtitle slot and, for richer phases, an additional small prose block above the .key-message) carries Maya's voice. Each phase narrative should:

  • Open with one sentence on what Maya is doing and why.
  • Show one concrete artifact verbatim in a .snippet block:
  • Phase 1 — the literal /3c-create-issue prompt she sends, then the resulting issue body (truncated to ~10 lines).
  • Phase 2 — the architect subagent's output snippet (3–4 bullet points), then the rule-file excerpt (.claude/rules/<rule>.md) Maya quotes back at it.
  • Phase 3 — the /3c-project-manager plan "<milestone>" invocation and its coherence report (one finding per check, 5 lines).

  • Phase 4 — the post-edit advisory exactly as shipped:

    3c post-edit validation found 1 issue(s) — please self-correct:
  - [layer-boundary] src/account/home/orders-panel.tsx:3 —
    "app" layer must not import from "infra" layer

    plus a JSONL gate event verbatim (one line). - Phase 5 — the layers / deny stanza of .3c/architecture.yaml the advisory was checked against, and the JSONL bypass event with the reason field populated. - Phase 6 — a 3c bug structured report header (5 lines, scrubbed). - Close with the three call-outs (as compact bullets, not boxes — the .key-message box already does the visual emphasis): - What 3C does for you here. - What Maya still owns here. (always a thinking / judgement action, never a typing action) - What 3C deliberately does NOT do here.

Cap each phase body copy at ~180 words so the page stays scannable and the diagram dominates.

docs.title: Closing page (page 9) — common mistakes + checklist
docs.text:
Two stacked sections inside the existing .closing layout:

Common mistakes — six cards (re-use the .takeaway-grid / .takeaway styles, but number them with a red .takeaway-num accent instead of indigo, and rename the class for the rendered file). Each card is one sentence on the mistake plus one sentence on the correction. Required mistakes:

  1. Rubber-stamping AI-generated issues; correction: read every issue body before publishing — /3c-create-issue produces what you prompt, not what you mean.
  2. Pasting the entire standards doc into prompts; correction: trust the .claude/rules/ library and the 150-instruction budget — re- pasting blows the budget and degrades the model.
  3. Bypassing without a real --reason; correction: the JSONL event is permanent and reviewable — "forgot why" in the reason field is how teams lose trust in the bypass mechanism.
  4. Treating boundary findings as noise; correction: a post-edit advisory is the architecture your team declared, not a style opinion — fix the direction, or change .3c/architecture.yaml on purpose.
  5. Running /3c-implement on issues that haven't been enriched; correction: enrich first (Phase 2), then implement — architect is cheaper before code than after.
  6. Trying to edit code or tests by hand to "save time"; correction: the assistant types, you instruct — every hand-edit is a missed opportunity for the rule library to evolve.

Pinnable checklist (single card spanning both columns, ≤ 20 lines). Required content, in this order:

  • Slash commands by phase: /3c-create-issue · /3c-project-manager · /3c-implement · /3c-test · /3c-review · 3c bug · 3c bypass --reason="...".
  • Subagents and when to dispatch each: architect (design call), security-reviewer (auth/crypto/input-handling), code-reviewer (pre-PR findings), test-author (writes the failing test inside /3c-test), product-owner (scope/priority), ux-expert (screen-level UX), qa-reviewer (AC traceability), journey-architect (journey reachability) — or convene all eight at once with /3c-review-board, which reconciles their findings into one verdict.
  • Gate chain in firing order: Post-Edit Validation (< 300 ms) → Pre-Commit (< 10 s) → Security Scan (< 60 s).
  • Bypass syntax: 3c bypass --reason="<one-line>" — logged, never silent.
  • File paths to remember: CLAUDE.md (root, ≤ 150 instructions), .claude/rules/<rule>.md, .3c/architecture.yaml, .3c/telemetry/hooks/*.jsonl, .3c/dashboard.html.
  • The one rule that summarises the rest: the assistant types, you instruct.

docs.title: Tone
docs.text:
